summary:
A crew planning a lunar habitat asks: which NASA fire results apply to our cabin? VESTA answers with evidence coverage, traced to its source.

Pick a cabin, a material and a concern (prevention, detection, suppression). VESTA checks 1,989 source-table rows from 24 NASA Physical Sciences Informatics combustion investigations against the cabin's gravity class, oxygen and pressure, and reports nearby evidence, evidence at other conditions, or no source in this collection. Every cited row opens its NASA record and shows what is assumed or missing.

For a lunar habitat (34% O2, 56.5 kPa, 1/6 g), 0 of 45 questions have a nearby row. It is not only gravity: the same oxygen and pressure in microgravity also give 0. On a station cabin 3 of 45 do, and all 24 matching rows rely on a pressure the tables never report. VESTA turns the gap into a request: one test campaign at the lunar cabin's conditions would give a nearby row to 23 of 45 questions.

From the rows it does have, VESTA shows one result: in FLEX droplet tests, flames went out on their own in 103/115 tests at 18% oxygen or less and 0/9 above 30%.

In a 3D lunar base, a simulated robot stages the review kit only after a person approves. No hardware, no live AI model, no safety prediction. Data, code, a static API and an MCP server are open.
details:
What it does. VESTA is an evidence-coverage checker for the challenge "Flame in Freefall". For a cabin atmosphere, a material and a fire concern it shows which NASA source-table rows are at nearby conditions, how the others differ, and what is missing.

How it works.

- Coverage: 15 cabin materials x 3 concerns = 45 questions. "Nearby" means one source row with the same gravity class, oxygen within 1 percentage point and pressure within 5 kPa. The tolerances are the team's choice; a sensitivity table shows the lunar result does not change at 2x or 4x.

- Sources: all 1,989 rows link to their NASA PSI investigation, with table file and row number. Rows are table records, not independent experiments.

- Assumptions: pressure is not reported in any of the 288 cabin-material rows. VESTA uses a nominal facility pressure from a NASA guide and labels it. Each row also lists what was recorded but is not compared: flow, specimen form and thickness.

- Outside the collection: the PSI tables are microgravity by design. VESTA lists NASA titles on Moon, Mars, partial or normal gravity that sit outside the tables, and says which it has read.

- Next requests: for each cabin, a ranked list of what a reviewer could request, with the nearest existing row and its exact distance.

- One result from the data: FLEX droplet extinction by ambient oxygen band (103/115, 63/91, 20/59, 0/9, with intervals). A logistic model on oxygen and fuel gets 179/224 held-out tests right against 150/224 for the majority baseline; its gain over a single oxygen cut (164/224) is not statistically clear, and VESTA says so. Liquid droplets in microgravity, not cabin materials.

- Space lab: an inventory review produces a source-linked request. After explicit approval, a simulated humanoid retrieves the review kit and stages it at the crew station. Changing the cabin revokes the approval.

- Trust: ten reproducible software checks, and a recorded review by an external Claude session that queried VESTA's local MCP server over the public data (12 read-only calls). No language model runs in the website.

Benefits. A habitat designer or researcher sees in minutes which questions have evidence near their conditions, which rest on an assumption, and which test would close the most gaps.

What is creative. The gap is the product: VESTA shows where the collected evidence stops, keeps every assumption visible, and gives the robot a job that follows from the evidence.

What we considered. "No source" means absent from this collection, not unstudied by NASA. Coverage is not a safety rating. Software tests are not scientific validation.

Tools. JavaScript ES modules, HTML, CSS, Three.js, Node.js tests (566 passing), Python for table normalization, Model Context Protocol server, GitHub Pages.

Also in the app. Ask the data: ten recorded answers written by our AI agents from the repository data and re-computed by a separate auditor agent, plus typed questions answered by fixed rules (no language model). NASA limiting-oxygen measurements at lunar and Martian gravity (Olson and Ferkul, 2012) shown with their source. Saffire-II samples compared between microgravity and normal gravity. A suit-pressure and cabin-oxygen panel built from three NASA documents.
